explain.say: A lithium-ion battery has two electrodes: a graphite anode and a metal oxide cathode, with a liquid electrolyte between them. Charging pushes lithium ions out of the cathode, through the electrolyte, and into the anode.

faq.q: What happens when you charge a lithium-ion battery?
faq.a: The charger pushes electrons into the anode and pulls lithium ions out of the cathode, through the electrolyte, to join them in the graphite. The energy from the charger is stored in this arrangement.
asks: How does charging a phone battery work?

faq.q: What is the anode made of?
faq.a: Usually graphite, a form of carbon made of thin flat sheets. Lithium ions slip in between the sheets when charging, and some newer batteries add silicon to hold more.

It is a thin plastic film full of tiny holes, letting lithium ions pass through the electrolyte while keeping the anode and cathode apart. If they touched, the battery would short-circuit and overheat.

faq.q: What is the cathode made of?
faq.a: A metal oxide containing lithium, such as lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide, or lithium iron phosphate. The choice decides how much energy the battery holds, how long it lasts and how safe it is.
asks: What metals are in a lithium battery?

faq.q: Why do lithium-ion batteries wear out?
faq.a: Each charge and discharge slowly damages the electrodes and builds up a thin crust that traps lithium. Heat, very fast charging and keeping the battery at 100 percent all speed this up.
asks: Why does my phone battery not last as long?

facts: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for developing lithium-ion batteries.
Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion batteries in 1991.
